doc.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]

title: The New York Times review and how Bucky's trio introduced songs
summary: Rowe reads a Times review about whimsy in his music. Pizzarelli says he borders on shtick, and recalls Bucky with John Bunch and Jay Leonhart.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: I have here an article from the New York Times it’s entitled — it’s a review — “A Family Reunion with a Smile” John Pizzarelli at the Regency. And I wanted to read just a short bit from it. This is a fellow named Steven Holden. He said, “For all the whimsy he weaves into his music, the jokes and references never devolve into comic shtick but embody his view of music-making as intellectual and aesthetic play.
That’s when they used to be able to write in the New York Times.

Well you know I think that’s — you know I think I still border on the shtick but I’ve gotten a little better at it, at the important times anyway. I mean I like the idea of, you know we used to joke with Bucky about, you know could you at least tell us what the next song is? Could we have a clue? Will you let us in? You know when he would do solo concerts when I was between ten and fifteen. But then when he worked with John Bunch and Jay Leonhart, they would let — Bucky would talk for a while and then he’d say, “John Bunch” and John would say, “Here’s what we’re going to do next.” You know they had a really nice little rhythm about what was going on and I think that’s what all © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
that stemmed out. And I think the other part was I like to tell little stories about the things that connected the dots a little bit.
Yeah it doesn’t get pedantic which I like because sometimes you feel oh they’re trying to teach you something now and you should know this.

And that’s a turn off. But I also just wanted to make an observation that I like the fact that you know you only have three musicians but sometimes people don’t realize that taking out an instrument or two adds another texture to the whole affair, and you all did that.
